resources.string: Frame format CoC values are suggestions and can be edited manually.
DOF diagram: near limit %1$s, focus point %2$s, far limit %3$s.
Local storage is temporarily unavailable. Try again.
A fully offline depth-of-field and hyperfocal distance calculator.
Local settings could not be saved. Try again.
A smaller CoC sets a stricter sharpness criterion and a smaller calculated depth of field.
Traditional depth of field based on frame format.
Assess sharpness when magnifying a digital image.
Sharpness under the chosen print viewing conditions.
Set the circle of confusion manually.

Traditional CoC values assume conventional photo viewing conditions, not pixel-level sharpness. Standard uses the linked catalogue recommendation; if none is given, it scales CoC with the physical frame diagonal. These are photographic assumptions, not absolute physical sharpness limits.

Uses square, evenly spaced pixels over the full physical frame area in the camera profile. MP is the actual recorded image resolution, not necessarily the nominal camera resolution. Crops and aspect-ratio changes may require a different physical area. The calculation uses pixel pitch and the chosen blur tolerance. It does not account for lens quality, demosaicing or diffraction, and does not guarantee the real resolving power of the optical system.

Uses the physical print size, viewing distance and angular blur tolerance. The exact tangent formula maps angular blur to a diameter on paper, then divides by image enlargement. Fit leaves margins if needed; Fill crops edges. A larger viewing distance allows more physical blur; a smaller angle is stricter. The 1–3 arcminute presets are photographic assumptions, not universal medical or photographic standards. File PPI and printer DPI are reference information and do not change optical CoC.
Enter a finite positive CoC in millimetres. Your value is stored with full precision independently of the camera profile.
Fit keeps the whole image with margins if needed. Fill covers the print area and crops if needed. Image orientation is matched automatically.
Check finite positive numbers and physical frame dimensions. Invalid or excessively large values are not used in calculations.
Sharpness of the final physical image on a display.

Print-Based now uses viewing distance and an angular blur criterion instead of file PPI and pixel blur. Your old settings remain archived. PPI is now reference information; printer DPI does not change optical depth of field.
PPI describes image pixels per inch and is used only to estimate file dimensions. DPI describes printer dots. Neither changes the visual CoC. Leave either field empty if not needed.
These presets are examples, not specifications of particular devices. All values remain editable. Square pixels are assumed.
Visual uses angular blur at the viewing distance. Display Pixels uses an explicit number of display pixels. They are separate alternatives and are never combined automatically.

Angular size describes the smallest blur assumed distinguishable at the viewing distance. A smaller angle is stricter. These photographic assumptions are not universal medical thresholds or absolute standards.
File for the full paper area: %1$s × %2$s px
Pixel counts are rounded up for file preparation. Fit may leave margins; the actual photograph size is shown separately. This reference does not change CoC.

Evaluates the physical image on a display using its size, viewing distance and chosen angular tolerance. Visual is independent of pixel density when physical size and aspect ratio stay unchanged. Display Pixels is a separate blur criterion. Fit shows the whole photograph; Fill crops it. Square pixels and matching frame orientation are assumed. These photographic assumptions do not guarantee real image detail, lens quality or a universal threshold of human vision.
This value is outside the supported calculation range.
At f/%1$s, diffraction may reduce the microcontrast of fine details.
At f/%1$s, the Airy disk reaches or exceeds the selected CoC.
At f/%1$s and %2$s, the estimated effective aperture is f/%3$s.
Without macro correction: automatic magnification is unavailable. Refine magnification manually.

Diffraction gradually reduces fine-detail contrast. Stopping down can still improve the overall scene sharpness by increasing depth of field. This approximate warning is not a requirement to open the aperture. Airy disk diameter and geometric defocus CoC describe different effects; their comparison is only a practical indicator. The 0.7 and 1.0 thresholds are app heuristics, not universal standards.
Enter A:B (1:2 = 0.5, 2:1 = 2) or a positive decimal value.
Enter a finite positive magnification or a valid A:B ratio.
Manual magnification applies only to its confirmed distance and nominal focal length.
At optical infinity, magnification is zero. The saved manual value is paused until finite focusing resumes.
Hyperfocal mode uses the actual focusing distance H for Auto estimation. The saved manual override is paused; it resumes in DOF at a finite distance.

Auto is an approximate thin-lens estimate from focal length and sensor-to-subject distance, limited to 0–1:1. It is unavailable below four focal lengths. Internal focusing, changing focal length, separated principal planes, extension tubes and close-up lenses can make it inaccurate. Use Manual for a known scale, including magnifications above 1:1.

Model: green light at 550 nm, ideal Airy disk and pupil ratio P = 1. Effective f-number is nominal f-number × (1 + m/P). Real asymmetric pupils may differ. Enter the nominal lens aperture: if the camera already displays a corrected effective f-number, this correction would count it twice and overestimate diffraction. Manual scale is exact as entered, but the diffraction model remains approximate.
Diffraction estimate unavailable for the current input.
No diffraction warning at the selected criterion.
Diffraction may limit detail at the selected sharpness criterion.
Set macro magnification instead of distance
Manual pairs a known magnification with a measured sensor-plane distance. Distance or focal changes require confirmation. Geometric depth of field continues to use nominal focal length.
Enter a finite positive scale and valid focal length. The estimated distance must be finite.
Focus follows the current hyperfocal distance when camera, sharpness, focal length or aperture changes.
Manual is tied to a measured distance. Changing the distance requires confirmation of the saved scale.
The right end of the slider sets optical infinity.
Depth of field based on recorded video resolution.

A geometric defocus criterion based on output recording pixels, not the physical sensor pixel pitch or measured camera detail. Auto takes the largest central sensor rectangle matching the video aspect ratio, then divides both sides by the additional linear crop. Manual area replaces Auto and ignores crop. Dimensions follow the camera profile axes; square output pixels are assumed. Oversampling, pixel binning, line skipping, sharpening and real video MTF are not modelled. Blur tolerance is a user choice, not a universal video standard.
Acceptable blur diameter in recorded video pixels. A smaller value sets a stricter criterion.
Additional linear crop relative to the sensor area already matched to video proportions. This is not a Full Frame crop factor and does not change the real focal length.
Enter the actual recording area in the profile axes. It must fit within the sensor and match the video aspect ratio (0.1% tolerance). Additional crop is not applied.
Manual area · additional crop is not applied
Enter a positive whole number of pixels (up to 2147483647).
Enter a finite positive blur tolerance in pixels.
Additional crop must be finite and at least 1.0×.
Enter finite positive active-area dimensions in millimetres.
The active area exceeds the selected sensor. Correct its dimensions or use Auto.
The active area does not match the video proportions. Correct its dimensions or use Auto.
Sensor dimensions are missing. Select a camera with known dimensions or edit its profile.
These values exceed the supported numeric range.
Distance from the sensor or film plane to the subject, not from the front lens.
This focal length is an equivalent in a simplified thin-lens model and can differ from the real lens. It never replaces nominal focal length in depth-of-field calculations.

The scale and distance give a thin-lens equivalent of %1$s mm versus a nominal %2$s mm (K = %3$s). Check the sensor-plane distance and magnification. These thresholds are app heuristics, not physical lens limits. You can confirm an unusual optical setup.
Distance changed. Update the magnification for this distance.
Nominal focal length changed. Check the saved magnification and distance.
Confirm the saved magnification for the current distance and lens before using Manual.
Enter a finite positive number. Both decimal separators are accepted.
These values cannot be calculated within the numeric range. Check the scale and distance.
Enter valid nominal focal length and aperture on the calculator.
At optical infinity, magnification is zero. The saved Manual pair is paused and must be checked before reuse.

The model uses the sensor-to-subject distance and coincident principal planes. Real lenses may have separated and moving principal planes, internal focusing, asymmetric pupils or additional optics. The equivalent focal length is not a measurement of the lens. Macro diffraction assumes nominal aperture and pupil ratio P = 1; a camera displaying an already corrected effective aperture can cause a double correction.
Focal length is shared with the calculator. Changes apply immediately.
Standard CoC for this format is automatically calculated from the frame diagonal, using 36×24 mm with CoC 0.030 mm as reference
Maximum Aperture at Wide End, f/
Maximum Aperture at Tele End, f/
All lenses contribute to quick values. No active lens selection is needed; manual input stays unrestricted.
Save the camera before adding lenses.
Maximum focal length must be greater than minimum focal length.
The minimum aperture f-number must be at least as large as both maximum aperture f-numbers.
Standard DOF may be approximate at close distances. The results remain useful for an approximate depth-of-field estimate.
This distance is very small relative to the nominal focal length. Macro photography is possible, but the simplified model cannot estimate magnification reliably.

Magnification is an approximate thin-lens estimate from nominal focal length and the sensor-to-subject distance. Internal focusing, changing focal length, separated principal planes, asymmetric optics, extension tubes, bellows and close-up lenses can cause substantial differences. Below four nominal focal lengths this model has no real solution; this does not make the distance impossible for a real lens.
Macro settings refine the actual magnification and diffraction estimate. DOF remains approximate; opening these settings does not switch to a separate macro DOF model.
